title: Add a Water Line
summary: Tee into an existing copper, PEX or CPVC line and run new PEX to a fridge, utility sink, outdoor hose bib or new fixture, ending at a stub-out with its own quarter-turn shutoff valve. Pressure tested and ready for inspection.
safety: Shut off and drain the water before cutting. Turn off power to any wall you drill into and look for wires and pipes first. Wear safety glasses when drilling. If soldering, follow the fire precautions in the copper pipe guide and keep the flame away from PEX.
pro: you also need a new drain or vent (any sink or fixture), the main shutoff won't close, the pipe is galvanized steel or brittle CPVC, the framing is engineered joists or trusses, or your area requires a licensed plumber. Adding a supply line often needs a permit; check local code.

steps.t: Check what this job covers and get a permit
steps.idea: Adding a supply line is often permit work, and some fixtures need much more than water.
steps.b:
1. Call or check the website of your building department. Ask: "Do I need a plumbing permit to add a water supply line?" Many areas say yes; some allow homeowner permits.
  2. Ask what inspection they want (usually before you cover the pipe) and how they want it pressure tested.
  3. Decide what you're feeding: {{a.use==='fridge'?'a fridge or ice maker':a.use==='sink'?'a utility sink':a.use==='hose'?'an outdoor hose bib':'a new fixture'}}.
  4. {{a.use==='sink'||a.use==='fixture'?'This guide covers the WATER SUPPLY only. A sink or fixture also needs a drain and a vent. Plan those first with a separate guide or a plumber; the drain location decides where the supply goes.':'An ice maker or hose bib needs no drain, so this guide covers the whole job.'}}
[[warn|Drains and vents|New drains and vents are not in this guide. Getting slope, traps and venting wrong causes sewer gas and slow drains. Call a plumber or use a drain guide.]]
faq: Can I skip the permit?
Unpermitted work can cause trouble with insurance claims and home sales. A supply line is a small permit and the inspection is quick.
Why add a valve at the end?
So you can shut off just this fixture to repair or replace it without shutting off the house.

steps.idea: Tap the nearest line of the right temperature that you can reach and cut safely.
steps.b:
1. Find a {{a.lines==='both'?'cold and a hot':'cold'}} line close to the new location: in the basement, crawlspace, or an open wall. Shorter runs mean better pressure and less work.
  2. Follow the line back: cold lines come from the main, hot lines come from the water heater's outlet. Feel them with the water running if you're unsure.
  3. Pick a straight section with at least 6" of clear pipe and room to get a cutter around it.
  4. Don't tee in after a water softener for an outdoor hose bib if you can avoid it (softened water is wasted on the lawn). For a fridge, either is fine.
  5. Don't tap the line right at the water heater, or a line feeding only a toilet if you can reach a bigger branch.
  6. Your current choice: tapping {{a.material.toUpperCase()}}, {{a.main}}" pipe.
faq: Can I tap a 1/2" line that feeds a bathroom?
Usually yes for a fridge or hose bib. A whole new bathroom needs a bigger line, which is designer work.
What about the saddle valve that came with my ice maker kit?
Don't use it. Self-piercing saddle valves clog and leak, and many codes don't allow them. A real tee is the right way.

steps.idea: A good route is short, protected, and stays out of cold spaces.
steps.b:
1. Sketch the path from the tee to the new spot. Go under the floor or through interior walls where you can.
  2. Avoid exterior walls in a cold climate. If you must use one, keep the pipe on the warm (inside) side of the insulation.
  3. Keep PEX at least 6" from a water heater flue and other hot surfaces, out of sunlight, and follow the PEX maker's rule for metal pipe near the water heater.
  4. Measure the route along the framing, including up and down. Enter it in the questions: {{a.run}} ft.
  5. Count the studs or joists you'll drill through: {{a.holes}}.
  6. Pick the stub-out height: for a fridge about 6"–12" above the floor, off to the side of the compressor; for a sink, follow the fixture's spec sheet (often about 20" above the floor, hot left, cold right).
faq: How much PEX should I buy?
The numbers above add 15% plus 3 ft for slack and mistakes, rounded to a common coil size.

steps.idea: All fittings must match one system: same PEX size and connection type.
steps.b:
1. Use the Tools list, which already matches your answers.
  2. Stick to one PEX connection type: {{a.join==='crimp'?'copper crimp rings':a.join==='clamp'?'stainless cinch clamps':'push-fit'}}. Mixing parts from different systems is how leaks happen.
  3. Read the PEX label: it should say "NSF-61" or "NSF-pw" (safe for drinking water) and the PEX type (A, B or C).
  4. Buy 2–3 spare fittings and rings. Returns are easier than a second trip mid-job.
  5. Practice: make two or three connections on a scrap of PEX before working on the house.
faq: Crimp, clamp or push-fit?
Crimp rings are cheapest but each tool fits only one size. Cinch clamps use one tool for all sizes. Push-fit needs no tool but costs more per fitting. All three work when done right.
My house has PEX-A (Uponor/ProPEX).
Most crimp, clamp and push-fit fittings are listed for PEX-A, B and C. Check the fitting package. Expansion fittings need their own expander tool.

steps.idea: Drill clean holes in the middle of studs and joists so the pipe runs straight and protected.
steps.b:
1. Before drilling into a wall, turn off power to outlets in that wall at the breaker. Look for wires and pipes with a flashlight.
  2. In studs: mark the center of the stud face. Drill straight through with a 3/4" or 7/8" bit. For hot+cold, drill two holes or one slightly larger.
  3. Keep stud holes small: in a load-bearing 2x4 wall, 1-3/8" or smaller and at least 5/8" from either face.
  4. In joists: drill near the middle of the joist's height, at least 2" from the top and bottom edges, and keep holes away from the ends.
  5. Where a hole is close to the face of a stud (any standard 2x4 wall), nail a steel plate over the face.
  6. Holes through a top or bottom plate between floors: seal around the pipe later with fire-rated caulk or foam.
steps.stop: Never cut or drill engineered I-joists or trusses without the maker's hole chart, and never notch the middle of a joist. Not sure what you're drilling? Stop and ask.
faq: Can I notch instead of drilling?
Avoid it. Notches weaken framing more than holes and are limited by code. Drill.
The drill won't fit between the studs.
Use a right-angle drill or a right-angle attachment, and a short auger bit.

steps.idea: Pull the PEX through the holes in one piece, with gentle bends and support every 32".
steps.b:
1. Uncoil the PEX by rolling the coil along the floor, not by pulling a loop off the side (that kinks it).
  2. Feed it through the holes from the stub-out end back toward the tee. {{a.lines==='both'?'Run red for hot and blue for cold.':'Use blue for cold.'}}
  3. Bend it gently: no tighter than about 6 times its outside diameter (about 4" for 1/2" PEX), or the maker's minimum.
  4. Clip it about every 32" along joists, snug but loose enough to slide (PEX grows as it warms).
  5. Leave a little slack at each end. Don't cut to length until the fittings are in hand.
  6. Cut with a PEX cutter, square and clean.
faq: I kinked it.
Cut out the kink and join the pieces with a coupling. Kinks restrict flow and can split later.
Can PEX touch the hot water pipe?
Keep PEX from touching other hot pipes and give it room to move so it doesn't rub on framing.
Can I run it outside?
No. Sunlight breaks PEX down. Keep it covered and indoors.

steps.idea: The end of the line must be screwed to solid wood so it can't move when you use the valve.
steps.b:
1. Screw a 2x4 block flat between the studs at the stub-out height, set back so the elbow's outlet ends near the drywall face.
  2. Screw the drop-ear elbow to the block (or clip the stub-out elbow into its bracket).
  3. Connect the PEX to the elbow (see the connection step for your method).
  4. Using an ice-maker box instead? Screw the box to the stud at the right height and connect the PEX to its valve.
  5. The valve goes on after the drywall is patched. Until then, cap the outlet for testing.
faq: The wall is already closed.
Cut a neat drywall opening between two studs, install blocking, and patch it after the inspection.

steps.idea: A frost-free hose bib keeps its valve inside the warm house and has a built-in anti-siphon device.
steps.b:
1. Pick a spot through the rim joist or wall, not over a window well or walkway.
  2. Choose a sillcock long enough that its valve end sits inside the heated space (measure the wall or rim thickness plus a few inches).
  3. Drill the hole from inside, tilting the drill slightly so the hole slopes down toward the outside.
  4. Bed the flange in exterior sealant, slide the sillcock in, and screw the flange to the siding or trim.
  5. Support the inside end so it keeps the slight downward slope to the outside.
  6. Connect the PEX to its inlet.
steps.stop: Hose connections must have backflow protection (a vacuum breaker or anti-siphon valve) so dirty water can't get sucked back into your drinking water. Buy a sillcock with it built in.
faq: Why does it need to slope?
So the water in the long stem drains out every time you shut it off. That's what keeps it from freezing.
Do I still need a shutoff inside?
It's a good idea: a quarter-turn valve inside lets you shut it off without shutting off the house. Check local code; some cold areas require one.

steps.t: Shut off the water and drain the line
steps.idea: The pipe you cut must be empty and depressurized.
steps.b:
1. Close the main shutoff valve (clockwise, or a lever across the pipe).
  2. Open the highest faucet in the house to let air in.
  3. Open the lowest tap to drain the lines. Wait until it stops.
  4. {{a.lines==='both'?'Tapping a hot line: set the water heater to VACATION/PILOT (gas) or turn off its breaker (electric).':'Check that no water flows from the cold faucets.'}}
  5. Put a bucket and towels under the tee location.
steps.stop: If the main valve won't turn or won't stop the water, don't force it. Call the water utility to close the curb valve, or a plumber.
faq: How long will the water be off?
Usually 30–60 minutes if everything is ready. Prepare all parts before you shut it off.

steps.idea: Remove just enough pipe for the tee, then join it like any copper fitting.
steps.b:
1. Hold the tee against the pipe. Mark where each socket's internal stop lines up: that's the gap to cut out.
  2. Cut at the first mark with the tubing cutter. Let the water drain into the bucket.
  3. Cut at the second mark. Deburr both ends inside and out.
  4. {{a.cjoin==='sweat'?'Clean and flux the ends and tee. Spring one pipe end sideways, slip the tee on, then line it up with the other end. Solder all three joints with the branch pointing toward your new line. Solder the copper-by-PEX adapter into the branch. Let it cool fully.':'Mark the insert depth on both pipe ends. Spring one pipe aside, push the tee onto one end, then line up the other and push it in to the mark.'}}
  5. If the pipe can't move sideways, cut a wider gap, put the tee on one end, add a short piece of pipe, and close the gap with a slip coupling.
faq: Can I solder with water dripping?
No. Open a lower faucet to drain it, or use push-fit fittings. The copper pipe guide covers this.
The tee isn't straight.
Rotate it before the solder cools, or before pushing fully on. Point the branch the way the PEX will run.

steps.idea: PEX flexes, so cutting in a tee is the easy case.
steps.b:
1. Check the old PEX type on its printing (PEX-A, B or C) and that your fittings are listed for it.
  2. Cut the PEX square with the PEX cutter.
  3. {{a.join==='push'?'Mark the insert depth on both ends.':'Slide a '+(a.join==='crimp'?'crimp ring':'cinch clamp')+' onto each cut end.'}}
  4. Flex the ends apart and insert the tee's run sockets. The pipe should bottom out on the fitting shoulder.
  5. Make the joints (see the connection step). Point the branch toward your new line.
faq: Can I remove a small piece?
Yes, if the pipe is tight. PEX is flexible enough to bend into a fitting without removing any length in most cases.

steps.idea: Older CPVC can be brittle, so cut gently and use a push-fit tee.
steps.b:
1. Cut the CPVC square with a ratcheting cutter or tubing cutter. Support the pipe; don't let it snap.
  2. Remove about the fitting's center gap so the tee fits.
  3. Deburr inside and out and chamfer the outside edge slightly so it doesn't cut the O-ring.
  4. Mark the insert depth on both ends and push the tee on, as in the push-fit step.
steps.stop: If the CPVC cracks or shatters when you cut it, it's brittle. Expect more breaks nearby. Cut back to sound pipe, and consider calling a plumber.
faq: Can I glue a CPVC tee instead?
Yes, with CPVC primer (where required) and CPVC cement, following the cure time on the can before pressure. Push-fit is easier for a first-timer.

steps.idea: A copper ring squeezed around the PEX locks it onto the fitting's barbs.
steps.b:
1. Cut the PEX square. Slide a copper crimp ring onto the tube.
  2. Push the PEX onto the fitting until it touches the shoulder.
  3. Slide the ring so its edge is 1/8"–1/4" from the end of the PEX.
  4. Put the tool jaws over the ring, square to the fitting, and squeeze the handles all the way closed.
  5. Test with the go/no-go gauge: the GO slot slides over the ring, the NO-GO slot must not.
steps.stop: If a crimp fails the gauge or is crooked, cut it off and redo it with a new ring. Never crimp a ring twice.
faq: The gauge says NO-GO slides on.
The crimp is too loose. Cut it off and redo. If it keeps happening, adjust your tool (most have a calibration screw).

steps.idea: A stainless cinch clamp squeezed by its ear locks the PEX onto the fitting.
steps.b:
1. Cut the PEX square. Slide a cinch clamp onto the tube.
  2. Push the PEX onto the fitting until it touches the shoulder.
  3. Slide the clamp so it's 1/8"–1/4" from the end of the PEX.
  4. Put the tool's jaws over the ear, square to the pipe, and squeeze until the tool releases on its own.
  5. Check the closed ear with the gauge that came with the tool.
faq: Can I use pliers?
No. The tool closes the ear to an exact width; pliers will under- or over-squeeze it.

steps.idea: Push the PEX in to the depth mark and it's sealed.
steps.b:
1. Cut the PEX square with a PEX cutter. No angle, no burrs.
  2. Check that the fitting has a stiffener for PEX (often pre-installed). If not, insert the one from the package.
  3. Mark the insert depth with the gauge.
  4. Push the PEX straight in until it hits the stop and the mark is at the fitting edge.
  5. Tug it back. It should not move out.
faq: Can I cut PEX with a utility knife?
No. It leaves an angled or ragged cut that can leak. Use a PEX cutter.

steps.t: Cap the end and pressure test
steps.idea: Prove every joint holds before anything gets covered up.
steps.b:
1. {{a.use==='hose'?'Close the new sillcock.':'Put the stop valve on the stub-out (or a test cap) and close it.'}}
  2. Close the lowest tap. Leave the top faucet open.
  3. Open the main a quarter of the way. When the top faucet runs steady without air, close it and open the main fully.
  4. Dry every joint. Hold dry tissue under each one for a minute.
  5. Check again after 30 minutes and again the next day. Everything must stay bone dry.
  6. If your inspector requires a gauge test, follow their numbers.
  7. Turn the water heater back on once its tank is full of water.
steps.stop: Any drip, even one drop, means the joint is wrong. Shut off, drain, cut it out and redo it. Don't close a wall over a joint you haven't watched for a day.
faq: A crimp ring weeps.
Cut it out and redo it with a new ring and a fresh cut of PEX.

steps.idea: Insulation prevents freezing and sweating; plates prevent future screws.
steps.b:
1. Slide foam sleeves over pipe in crawlspaces, garages, attics and any exterior wall. Slit side down.
  2. Tape the seams and the joints between sleeves.
  3. Insulate hot lines too, to save energy and wait time.
  4. Check that every stud hole near a wall face has a nail plate.
  5. Seal holes through top or bottom plates with fire-rated caulk or foam.
faq: Do I need to insulate in a heated basement?
Not for freezing, but cold lines may sweat in summer. Insulating them stops drips.

steps.idea: The inspector sees the pipe before it disappears into the wall.
steps.b:
1. Schedule the inspection with the pipe exposed and under pressure, if a permit was required.
  2. After it passes, patch the drywall around the stub-out.
  3. {{a.use==='hose'?'Seal the sillcock flange to the siding.':'Install the escutcheon (cover ring) and the quarter-turn stop valve on the stub-out. Tighten compression nuts one more turn past hand-tight, no more.'}}
  4. Turn on the water and check the valve for leaks.
faq: How tight is a compression nut?
Hand-tight, then about one more half to full turn with a wrench while holding the valve body with a second wrench.

steps.idea: Connect the appliance or fixture and flush out debris and air.
steps.b:
1. {{a.use==='fridge'?'Connect the braided supply line to the 1/4" valve outlet and to the fridge. Leave a loop of slack so the fridge can roll out.':a.use==='hose'?'Attach a hose and run water for a minute to flush.':'Connect the fixture\'s supply lines to the stop valve outlets.'}}
  2. Open the valve slowly. Check both ends for drips with dry tissue.
  3. {{a.use==='fridge'?'Throw away the first few batches of ice and run water through the dispenser per the fridge manual to flush the filter.':a.use==='hose'?'In winter, always take the hose off the sillcock so it can drain.':'Run the water for a minute with aerators removed, then put them back.'}}
  4. Check under the fixture again the next day.
faq: The ice maker isn't making ice.
Most need 24 hours to start. Check that the valve is fully open and the fridge's water filter is installed correctly.

crimpHelp.b:
1. Square cut. Ring on.
  2. PEX fully onto the fitting.
  3. Ring 1/8"–1/4" from the PEX end.
  4. Jaws square, squeeze fully.
  5. GO slides on, NO-GO doesn't.

clampHelp.b:
1. Square cut. Clamp on.
  2. PEX fully onto the fitting.
  3. Clamp 1/8"–1/4" from the PEX end.
  4. Tool on the ear, squeeze until it releases.
  5. Check with the gauge.

pushHelp.b:
1. Square, clean cut.
  2. Stiffener in place for PEX.
  3. Mark insert depth.
  4. Push to the mark. Tug to check.

I-joists: maker's chart only.</text><text x="84" y="62" class="wa">2"</text>
joist.cap: The top and bottom edges of a joist carry the load. Drill through the middle, away from the ends, and keep holes apart from each other.

bend.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Bend gently, never kink</text><path d="M30 40 V110 A40 40 0 0 0 70 150 H140" class="good" style="stroke-width:6" fill="none"/><text x="30" y="176" class="gd">right: radius 6x OD</text><text x="30" y="188">(about 4" for 1/2" PEX)</text><path d="M190 40 V140 L200 150 H290" class="bad" style="stroke-width:6" fill="none"/><circle cx="194" cy="146" r="8" class="o"/><text x="190" y="176" class="wa">wrong: kinked</text><text x="190" y="188">cut it out and redo</text>
bend.cap: Tighter than the maker's minimum radius? Use a bend support or an elbow fitting. A kink restricts flow and can split later.

support.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Support it every 32"</text><rect x="10" y="30" width="300" height="14" class="w"/><line x1="10" y1="90" x2="310" y2="90" class="o" style="stroke:var(--mem);stroke-width:5"/><path d="M34 44 V84 a6 6 0 0 0 12 0 V44" class="o"/><path d="M154 44 V84 a6 6 0 0 0 12 0 V44" class="o"/><path d="M274 44 V84 a6 6 0 0 0 12 0 V44" class="o"/><line x1="60" y1="112" x2="140" y2="112" class="a"/><polygon points="140.0,112.0 133.7,115.0 133.7,109.0" class="af"/><line x1="140" y1="112" x2="60" y2="112" class="a"/><polygon points="60.0,112.0 66.3,109.0 66.3,115.0" class="af"/><text x="100" y="128" class="ac" text-anchor="middle">32" max</text><line x1="180" y1="112" x2="260" y2="112" class="a"/><polygon points="260.0,112.0 253.7,115.0 253.7,109.0" class="af"/><line x1="260" y1="112" x2="180" y2="112" class="a"/><polygon points="180.0,112.0 186.3,109.0 186.3,115.0" class="af"/><text x="220" y="128" class="ac" text-anchor="middle">32" max</text><text x="10" y="156">Plastic PEX clips or hangers, snug, not tight.</text><text x="10" y="168">Leave a little slack: PEX grows when hot.</text>
support.cap: Horizontal PEX gets a hanger about every 32" (the common code and maker spacing; check your local code). On vertical runs, support it at each floor.

heater.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Keep PEX away from heat</text><rect x="30" y="70" width="80" height="120" rx="8" class="tb"/><text x="70" y="136" text-anchor="middle">gas water</text><text x="70" y="148" text-anchor="middle">heater</text><rect x="62" y="24" width="16" height="46" class="bk"/><text x="84" y="34">flue</text><line x1="96" y1="70" x2="96" y2="40" class="o" style="stroke-width:5"/><line x1="96" y1="40" x2="170" y2="40" class="o" style="stroke-width:5"/><line x1="170" y1="40" x2="300" y2="40" class="o" style="stroke:var(--mem);stroke-width:5"/><text x="110" y="62" class="k">metal first</text><text x="110" y="74">(often 18")</text><text x="190" y="62" class="k">then PEX</text><text x="130" y="110" class="wa">PEX at least 6" from the flue,</text><text x="130" y="122">more if the maker says so.</text><text x="130" y="150">Keep it off recessed lights,</text><text x="130" y="162">out of sunlight, away from</text><text x="130" y="174">other hot surfaces.</text>
heater.cap: Most PEX makers want a stretch of metal pipe at a gas water heater and clearance from the flue. Follow your PEX brand's instructions; they are part of the code.

stubout.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Stub-out: anchored, then a valve</text><rect x="10" y="40" width="20" height="150" class="w"/><rect x="200" y="40" width="20" height="150" class="w"/><rect x="30" y="100" width="170" height="20" class="w"/><text x="165" y="114" text-anchor="middle">2x blocking</text><rect x="230" y="40" width="10" height="150" class="b"/><text x="244" y="36">drywall</text><path d="M120 190 V92" class="o" style="stroke:var(--mem);stroke-width:5"/><rect x="112" y="80" width="18" height="16" rx="2" class="tb"/><rect x="106" y="94" width="30" height="5" class="tb"/><line x1="130" y1="88" x2="262" y2="88" class="o" style="stroke-width:5"/><rect x="262" y="78" width="26" height="20" rx="3" class="tb"/><rect x="288" y="82" width="20" height="12" rx="2" class="y"/><text x="36" y="32" class="k">drop-ear elbow screwed to blocking</text><text x="246" y="118">stop valve</text><text x="246" y="130">goes on</text><text x="246" y="142">after drywall</text>
stubout.cap: The elbow is screwed to solid blocking so the pipe can't push back into the wall when you tighten the valve.

crimp.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Crimp ring: place, squeeze, gauge</text><rect x="10" y="60" width="120" height="30" rx="2" class="tb"/><text x="40" y="54">fitting</text><rect x="90" y="56" width="160" height="38" rx="4" class="m"/><text x="222" y="50" text-anchor="middle">PEX</text><rect x="108" y="52" width="14" height="46" rx="2" class="w"/><line x1="90" y1="104" x2="108" y2="104" class="o"/><text x="60" y="120" class="ac">ring 1/8"-1/4" from the PEX end</text><g><path d="M100 30 L115 48 L130 30" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><animateTransform attributeName="transform" type="translate" values="0 -6;0 0;0 -6" dur="1.8s" repeatCount="indefinite"/></g><g><path d="M100 120 L115 102 L130 120" class="o" style="stroke-width:3" opacity="0"/></g><rect x="20" y="140" width="120" height="30" rx="4" class="y"/><rect x="36" y="140" width="22" height="16" class="bk"/><rect x="96" y="140" width="18" height="16" class="bk"/><text x="47" y="184" class="gd" text-anchor="middle">GO: slides on</text><text x="140" y="184" class="wa">NO-GO: must not</text><text x="160" y="158">Fails? Cut off and redo.</text>
crimp.title: Crimp a PEX ring
crimp.cap: Push the PEX fully onto the fitting, slide the copper ring 1/8"–1/4" back from the end, crimp with the jaws square, then check every ring with the go/no-go gauge.

cinch.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Cinch clamp: squeeze the ear</text><rect x="10" y="66" width="110" height="28" rx="2" class="tb"/><rect x="80" y="60" width="180" height="40" rx="4" class="m"/><rect x="100" y="56" width="16" height="48" rx="2" class="bk"/><path d="M102 56 v-10 h12 v10" class="o"/><text x="124" y="40" class="k">ear: tool closes it flat</text><text x="10" y="128">1  PEX fully on the fitting.</text><text x="10" y="142">2  Clamp 1/8"-1/4" from the PEX end.</text><text x="10" y="156">3  Squeeze until the tool releases.</text><text x="10" y="170">4  Check with the gauge.</text>
cinch.cap: Stainless cinch clamps use one ratcheting tool for every size. The tool releases by itself when the clamp is done.

pushpex.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Push-fit on PEX: insert, mark, push</text><rect x="170" y="54" width="110" height="60" rx="6" class="tb"/><line x1="230" y1="54" x2="230" y2="114" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><rect x="30" y="68" width="200" height="32" rx="2" class="m"/><rect x="186" y="74" width="44" height="20" class="bk"/><line x1="170" y1="62" x2="170" y2="106" class="o" style="stroke-width:3"/><text x="208" y="136" class="k" text-anchor="middle">stiffener insert</text><text x="208" y="148" text-anchor="middle">(often built in)</text><text x="30" y="136" class="gd">depth mark at edge</text><text x="10" y="170">Square cut, mark depth, push until the mark meets it.</text>
pushpex.cap: PEX is soft, so the fitting needs a stiffener inside the tube to seal. Most brass push-fit fittings come with one already in place; check the package.

valve.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Quarter-turn stop valve</text><rect x="40" y="70" width="90" height="30" rx="6" class="tb"/><g><rect x="80" y="40" width="10" height="34" rx="3" class="y"/><animateTransform attributeName="transform" type="rotate" values="0 85 72;0 85 72;-90 85 72;-90 85 72;0 85 72" keyTimes="0;0.3;0.5;0.8;1" dur="4s" repeatCount="indefinite"/></g><text x="40" y="124" class="gd">Handle in line</text><text x="40" y="136">with the outlet = ON</text><text x="180" y="64" class="wa">Handle across</text><text x="180" y="76">the outlet = OFF</text><text x="180" y="104" class="k">Outlet size: 1/4"</text><text x="180" y="116">(fridge), 3/8" (sink)</text><text x="10" y="170">Compression, push-fit or PEX inlet to match.</text>
valve.title: Quarter-turn valve
valve.cap: Quarter-turn (ball) valves open or close with a 90° turn and are far more reliable than old multi-turn valves.

sillcock.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Frost-free sillcock, sloped to drain</text><rect x="140" y="30" width="40" height="150" class="b"/><text x="160" y="196" text-anchor="middle">wall</text><rect x="140" y="30" width="40" height="150" class="th" opacity=".35"/><g transform="rotate(4 160 100)"><rect x="40" y="94" width="210" height="12" rx="2" class="tb"/><rect x="250" y="88" width="30" height="24" rx="3" class="tb"/><rect x="270" y="74" width="14" height="14" rx="2" class="y"/></g><rect x="34" y="90" width="12" height="20" class="badf" opacity=".5"/><text x="10" y="72" class="k">valve seat: inside,</text><text x="10" y="84">in the warm house</text><text x="196" y="60">outside</text><text x="10" y="140">Slope down to outside</text><text x="10" y="152">so it drains when</text><text x="10" y="164">you shut it off.</text><text x="196" y="140" class="gd">Built-in vacuum</text><text x="196" y="152">breaker (anti-siphon)</text>
sillcock.cap: The long stem puts the actual valve inside the heated house. Remove the hose in winter or the trapped water can freeze and split it.

insulate.svg: <text x="10" y="16" class="k">Insulate in cold or unheated spaces</text><rect x="20" y="60" width="280" height="36" rx="18" class="th"/><rect x="20" y="72" width="280" height="12" rx="2" class="mos"/><line x1="20" y1="60" x2="300" y2="60" class="o d"/><text x="20" y="50" class="k">foam sleeve, slit side down</text><text x="20" y="116">tape the seams and the joints</text><text x="20" y="144">Also insulate hot lines to save energy.</text><text x="20" y="156">Keep pipes on the warm side of wall insulation.</text>
insulate.cap: Foam sleeves stop sweating on cold lines and slow freezing. In a cold climate, keep new lines out of exterior walls whenever you can.

glossary: PEX
Cross-linked polyethylene: flexible plastic water tubing. Red, blue and white are the same material.
Tee
A T-shaped fitting that splits one line into two.
Stub-out
The end of a supply line coming out of the wall, where the shutoff valve goes.
Drop-ear elbow
A 90° fitting with a flat tab you screw to wood, to anchor a stub-out.
Quarter-turn stop valve
A shutoff valve that opens or closes with a 90° turn of the handle.
Crimp ring
A copper ring squeezed around PEX to hold it on a fitting.
Cinch clamp
A stainless steel clamp with an ear that's squeezed flat to hold PEX on a fitting.
Go/no-go gauge
A slotted tool that checks a crimp is the right size.
Nail plate
A steel plate nailed over a stud where a pipe passes close to the face, to stop screws and nails.
Sillcock / hose bib
An outdoor faucet for a hose.
Vacuum breaker
A backflow device that stops hose water from being sucked back into the house pipes.
Slip coupling
A coupling with no internal stop, so it slides along the pipe to close a gap.
Fire-blocking
Sealing holes between floors so fire and smoke can't travel through them.
